title: Portia and the Pound of Flesh
text:
To help his friend Bassanio, the Venetian merchant Antonio borrowed three thousand ducats from the moneylender Shylock, who hated him. The terms were strange: if the money was not repaid on time, Shylock could cut a pound of flesh from Antonio's body. Antonio's ships were lost at sea, he could not pay, and Shylock took him to court before the Duke of Venice to claim his bond.

Bassanio's new wife, Portia, came to the court disguised as a young doctor of law. She first appealed to Shylock to show mercy. He refused. Bassanio offered to repay the money many times over. Shylock refused that too. He wanted only what the contract gave him. Portia agreed that the bond was valid and that Venetian law could not set it aside. Shylock sharpened his knife.

Then Portia stopped him. The bond, she said, gave him a pound of flesh, but not a single drop of blood. If he shed even one drop of a Christian's blood in taking it, his lands and goods would be confiscated. And he must cut exactly one pound, no more and no less, or he would die.

Shylock, defeated, asked for his money instead and was refused. Portia then turned the law against him further, and he left the court stripped of his fortune and forced to convert. Antonio was saved.
lesson: If the other side insists on the letter of an agreement, read the letter more carefully than they did. Precise terms cut both ways.
people: Portia, Shylock, Antonio, Bassanio, the Duke of Venice
source: William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, Act 4, Scene 1
caveat: The play's treatment of Shylock reflects the antisemitism of its time and is read critically today.
